description: Not independently attested in folklore literature. The name 'Cheval Mal Fet' garbles 'Le Chevaler Mal Fet' — 'the ill-made knight' — the epithet of Lancelot in Arthurian romance, popularized by T. H. White's novel 'The Ill-Made Knight.' No phantom horse or Haitian or Belgian ghost-horse tradition by this name is documented.
source: Arthurian romance tradition (Lancelot epithet); T. H. White, The Once and Future King
research_notes: Name is Lancelot's alias, not a horse; Haiti/Belgium phantom-horse legend fabricated.

description: Not independently attested in folklore literature. No Kazakh mountain-dwarf spirit named 'Chichkhan' appears in any collection of Kazakh or Central Asian Turkic folklore. Kazakh animistic tradition does describe yer-su earth-water spirits, divs, and witch-figures such as Zheztyrnak, but none matches this name.
research_notes: No source found for a Kazakh 'Chichkhan'; generic yer-su filler with no basis.

description: Not independently attested in folklore literature. No Uzbek cave spirit named 'Chil-kuyz' is recorded. Uzbek and broader Turkic tradition instead names harmful spirits such as albasti and the iye (yeys) household and nature guardians; 'Chil-kuyz' appears to be an invented blend of these figures.
research_notes: Real Uzbek/central Asian names are albasti, martu, iye/yeys; 'Chil-kuyz' unattested.

description: Not independently attested in folklore literature. 'Cholula' is the name of a city in Puebla, Mexico, not a folkloric being. The giant tradition attached to its great pyramid belongs to Xelhua, a Nahua survivor of the Fourth-Sun flood who climbed Mount Tlaloc and, in early colonial accounts, raised the pyramid of Tlachihualtepetl.
research_notes: Attested pyramid-building giant is Xelhua; no tradition names a giant 'Cholula'.

description: Not independently attested in folklore literature. 'Chupacora' is an unattested variant of the chupacabra, a livestock-killing cryptid first reported in Puerto Rico in 1995 and since reported across Latin America. No distinct Guatemalan 'Chupacora' with its own characteristics is documented.
research_notes: Invented variant; the genuine figure is the chupacabra (Puerto Rico, 1995).

description: The Ciguapa is a nocturnal wild woman of Dominican mountain folklore whose backward-turned feet baffle trackers. The earliest written account is Francisco Javier Angulo Guridi's 1866 story 'La Ciguapa.' Scholars debate a possible Taíno origin against European parallels such as mermaids and the churel.
source: F. J. Angulo Guridi, 'La Ciguapa' (1866); Dominican oral tradition
research_notes: Real figure (Angulo Guridi 1866); removed broken template filler 'known among the Dominican Republic people.'

description: Not independently attested in folklore literature. No cougar or puma deity appears in the documented Muisca pantheon of the Colombian Altiplano. Colonial records of the 1563 Ubaque ceremony mention a 'tiger' — perhaps a puma or jaguar — tied to the culture-hero Bochica, but no cave-guardian cougar deity is attested.
source: Colonial Muisca records; Ubaque ceremony account (1563)
research_notes: Bochica-1563 big-cat link is thin; cougar deity and Bachue underworld-guardian role invented.

description: Not independently attested in folklore literature. No cougar deity is recorded in Maliseet (Wolastoqiyik) tradition, and cougars were not established in Wabanaki territory. The Maliseet culture hero is Koluskap (Glooscap), the transformer of Wabanaki myth; the cougar sky-guardian role described is fabricated.
research_notes: Koluskap/Glooscap is real; cougar deity and sky-guardian role fabricated.

description: In the Numic traditions of the Great Basin, the legend 'The Wolf, the Fox, the Bobcat and the Cougar' tells how these four animal spirits helped the Shoshone-Bannock and related Paiute peoples defeat the Nimerigar, cannibalistic little people who shot poisoned arrows. The cougar appears as a heroic spirit ally, not a deity.
source: Shoshone-Paiute oral tradition; 'The Wolf, the Fox, the Bobcat and the Cougar'
research_notes: Nimerigar defeat tale is attested for Shoshone/Paiute; dropped inflated 'deity' and medicine-bundle framing.

description: Not independently attested in folklore literature. Cougars are not native to West Africa and no cougar deity exists in Yoruba cosmology. The genuine feline symbol is ekun, the leopard, totem of royalty and of the thunder god Shango, who is depicted wearing leopard skin; the entry conflates a cougar with this leopard symbolism.
research_notes: Explicit conflation of cougar with ekun (leopard); no cougar being in Yoruba tradition.

description: Not independently attested in folklore literature. Choctaw tradition does include the panther (koi) as a clan animal and the horned serpent Sint Holo as a water spirit, but no 'cougar ghost' guarding river crossings is documented. The river-threshold guardian role is invented.
research_notes: Panther clan and Sint Holo are real; 'cougar ghost' river-guardian is fabricated.

description: Not independently attested in folklore literature. No Lakota tradition describes a cougar 'ghost' or a 'lone warrior' mountain-lion spirit as narrated here. Lakota oral tradition features animal powers sought in vision quests, but this specific cougar-spirit figure and its symbolism have no documented source.
research_notes: No attested 'lone warrior' cougar spirit; generic symbolic padding.

description: Not independently attested in folklore literature. Choctaw emergence tradition holds that the people came from the underworld through the mound of Nanih Waiya, but no 'cougar giant' dwelling beneath it or causing earthquakes appears in any recorded tradition. The being is fabricated.
research_notes: Nanih Waiya emergence is real; earthquake-making cougar giant is invented.

description: Not independently attested in folklore literature. Cougars are not native to Africa, and no Kikuyu tradition describes giant spirit-cats guarding the lakes of Mount Kenya. Kikuyu cosmology centers on Ngai, the supreme god of Kirinyaga; the marozi, a spotted-lion cryptid of the Aberdares, is a separate and unverified notion.
research_notes: Cougars absent from Africa; 'giant spirit cats' guarding Mount Kenya lakes are invented.

description: Not independently attested in folklore literature. Kwakwaka'wakw (Kwakiutl) cosmology includes Dzunukwa the wild woman, Bakwas the ghost king, and Sisiutl the sea serpent, but no cougar giant figures among the transformation beings of the winter ceremonials. The cougar-giant role is invented.
research_notes: Dzunukwa/Bakwas/Sisiutl are real; cougar giant as ceremonial transformation being is fabricated.

description: In Shoshone oral tradition, the legend 'The Wolf, the Fox, the Bobcat and the Cougar' recounts how four animal spirits helped the Shoshone-Bannock defeat the Nimerigar, warlike little people of the Rocky Mountains who shot poisoned arrows. The cougar here is a heroic spirit ally, not a giant or mountain guardian.
source: Shoshone oral tradition; 'The Wolf, the Fox, the Bobcat and the Cougar'
research_notes: Nimerigar legend is attested; removed fabricated 'giant' status and mountain-pass guardian role.

description: Not independently attested in folklore literature. No Ute tradition records a cougar giant or a mountain-lion spirit with fixed color and season attributes. Ute mythology centers on Sinawav the creator and a circle of major animal spirits, but no cougar being matching this entry is documented.
research_notes: Color/season cougar symbolism invented; no attested Ute cougar spirit being.

description: Not independently attested in folklore literature. Cougars are not native to Balochistan. The genuine feline of Iranian-plateau tradition is the palang (leopard), a term rich in Persian literary symbolism (Rustam's leopard-skin), along with babr (tiger); the cave-guardian 'cougar' is invented.
research_notes: Conflates cougar with palang (leopard) and babr (tiger); cave-cat guardian is invented.

description: In Creek (Muscogee) tradition the panther is honored through the Panther Clan, Katsalgi, one of the principal matrilineal clans of the Creek Confederacy. Panther hunting medicine was highly regarded, and among the related Seminole the Panther clan is the premier medicinal clan.
source: Creek oral tradition; Hodge, Handbook of American Indians North of Mexico (1906)
research_notes: Katsalgi (Panther) clan attested; removed invented boundary-guardian framing.

description: Not independently attested in folklore literature. Coyote is not a Haida figure; the Haida trickster and transformer is Raven (Yáahl). The claim of a coyote brother of Raven who shaped the coastline is fabricated, importing a Plains and Great Basin trickster into Haida Gwaii.
research_notes: Raven is the Haida trickster; coyote deity and brother-of-Raven role entirely fabricated.

description: Not independently attested in folklore literature. Coyotes are not native to Kazakhstan, and no Kazakh failed-shaman 'coyote ghost' or 'Iyt-Köz' appears in any recorded tradition. Kazakh folklore reveres the wolf as legendary ancestor; the dog-eyed wanderer here is an invented figure.
research_notes: Coyotes absent from Kazakhstan; 'Iyt-Köz' failed-shaman ghost is entirely invented.

description: Yurok cosmology, recorded by A. L. Kroeber, places 'a gigantic white coyote and his yellow mate' at the head of the river in the sky, where the White Deerskin Dance is danced nightly. The celestial white coyote is a genuine Yurok being, distinct from the trickster Wohpekumew; the 'ghost' framing is not.
source: A. L. Kroeber, Yurok Myths (University of California Press, 1976)
research_notes: White-coyote sky cosmology attested (Kroeber); removed invented 'ghost' and moon-howling framing.

description: Not independently attested in folklore literature. No Yurok narrative describes a giant coyote carving the Klamath canyon or the redwood forests. The attested Yurok coyote figures are the celestial white coyote of the sky world (Kroeber) and the trickster Wohpekumew; the land-shaping giant is fabricated.
source: A. L. Kroeber, Yurok Myths (University of California Press, 1976)
research_notes: Coyote giant with body-turned-landscape is fabricated; only celestial white coyote attested.

description: Not independently attested in folklore literature. Coyotes are not native to Balochistan. The mountain wolf, gurg-e-koh, belongs to genuine regional lore, but a water-finding coyote guardian watching over dry riverbeds is invented; no Balochi source records it.
research_notes: 'Gurg-e-Koh' is a wolf, not a coyote; water-finding guardian role is invented.

description: Not independently attested in folklore literature. Cheyenne tradition features the trickster Wihio, the Thunder Spirit Nonoma, and the sacred arrows (Maahotse) brought by Sweet Medicine, but no coyote guardian who discovered the arrows is recorded. The guardian role is invented.
research_notes: Wihio/Nonoma/Maahotse are real; coyote guardian who found the sacred arrows is invented.

description: Not independently attested in folklore literature. Coyotes are not native to Myanmar, and no Burmese coyote guardian exists; the given description is a Swahili coastal invention ('Mlinzi wa Barabara'). Genuine Burmese guardian spirits are the nats, not coyote beings.
research_notes: Description was about Swahili/Kenya, not Burma; 'Mlinzi wa Barabara' is invented; nats are the real Burmese spirits.

description: Devi, the Great Goddess of Hinduism, is the supreme feminine power, Shakti. Her gentle forms include Parvati, Uma, and Gauri; her fierce forms include Durga, the ten-armed warrior who slays the buffalo demon Mahishasura, and Kali. The Devi Mahatmya of the Markandeya Purana recounts these victories.
research_notes: Goddess facts accurate; removed template filler. Entry metadata (type 'ogre') still mismatched.

description: Not independently attested in folklore literature. In Virgil's Aeneid (Book IV), Dido curses Aeneas and his Roman descendants, foretelling eternal enmity between Carthage and Rome before killing herself. No tradition describes her ghost haunting Carthage's ruins or a 'Carthaginian Curse' placed on the site.
research_notes: Attested Dido curse targets Aeneas/Rome (Aeneid IV); ghost haunting ruins and 'lament on the wind' invented.

description: Divs are demonic beings of Afghan folk tradition, part of the wider Persianate belief descended from Zoroastrian daevas. In Dari and Pashto tales divs dwell in remote mountains and caves, guard treasure, and abduct travelers, and heroes must outwit or overpower them. The Afghan div tradition is real, though details vary locally.
research_notes: Div belief real; condensed generic padding and removed invented named landmarks.

description: Divs (Persian: dīv, from Avestan daeva) are demonic beings of Iranian tradition, demonized in Zoroastrianism from older Indo-Iranian deities. In Ferdowsi's Shahnameh they are the chief antagonists of Rostam, including Div-e Sepid, the White Div who blinded King Kay Kavus, and Akvan-e Div.
research_notes: Replaced copied Afghan-div text with correct Iranian content (Shahnameh, Div-e Sepid, Akvan-e Div).

description: In Persian epic and folk tradition, divs are monstrous, night-active demons of inverted nature, descendants of Zoroastrian daevas. The Shahnameh portrays them as adversaries of the hero Rostam, most famously Div-e Sepid, whose blood restores the blinded king's sight. Folklore warns of divs lurking near villages after dark.
research_notes: Same duplicated Afghan text corrected to Persian epic content; distinguished from the Iran entry.

description: Dokkaebi are goblin-like spirits of Korean folklore, born from old household objects imbued with spiritual energy. Neither wholly good nor evil, they reward kindness and punish greed, wield the wish-granting bangmangi club, excel at ssireum wrestling, and can be warded off by horse blood or a hanging sieve.
source: National Folk Museum of Korea; Korean oral tradition
research_notes: Removed template filler 'known among the North Korea people.'

description: Doña Sebastiana is a New Mexican Hispano death figure — a skeletal woman with bow and arrows in a wooden cart, whose rattling is heard before a death. Carved as bultos in the santero tradition, she is identified with Santa Muerte in some stories and in others a separate figure who grants sinners a final confession.
source: Santero tradition of New Mexican folk art
research_notes: Real figure; fixed 'snip in others' artifact and condensed padding.

description: The Douen is a forest spirit of Trinidad and Tobagonian folklore, the soul of an unbaptized child who died and now wanders the woods. Its backward-turned feet confuse trackers, and it lures children away by mimicking the voices of parents and loved ones. Parents use Douen tales to keep children from wandering alone.
research_notes: Was copy-pasted Slavic Domovoy text; rewritten with real Douen content.

description: The Drac is a shapeshifting water spirit of southern French folklore, bound to the Rhône and neighboring rivers. Described by Gervase of Tilbury in the Otia Imperialia (c. 1213), dracs float gold rings or cups to lure people, drag nursing women below to raise their young, and can be repelled by the sign of the cross.
source: Gervase of Tilbury, Otia Imperialia; Paul Sébillot, Le Folk-Lore de France (1904)
research_notes: Was copy-pasted Douen text; rewritten with attested Provençal Drac content.

description: Drache is the German word for dragon. In Germanic folklore the Drache is a fire-breathing serpent or reptile guarding treasure in mountains, caves, and forests, with regional forms such as the Lindwurm. In the Nibelungenlied, Siegfried slays the dragon and bathes in its blood to become invulnerable.
research_notes: Was copy-pasted French Drac text; rewritten with real German Drache content.

description: Not independently attested in folklore literature. No Brunei legend names a 'Naga Berani' guarding Brunei Bay, and the celestial-guardian and sunken-kingdom details are unattested. Naga serpent-dragon motifs are real across Malay folklore and appear in Brunei's epic of Awang Semaun, but not as this specific bay dragon.
research_notes: No attested 'Naga Berani of Brunei Bay'; invented celestial-guardian and sunken-kingdom details.

description: The Drakaina is the feminine form of the drakon in Greek mythology — a serpent or serpent-woman of chthonic power. Notable drakainai include Echidna, mother of monsters; Campe, guardian of Tartarus slain by Zeus; and Delphyne, the serpent who guarded Zeus' umbilical cord and was killed by Apollo.
research_notes: Was copy-pasted German Drache text; rewritten with attested Greek Drakaina content.

description: In modern Greek folk tradition, drakos (pl. drakoi) are monstrous, ogre-like giants, distinct from the classical drakon. Dragon-slayer tales, including the Akritas cycles, recount heroes battling drakoi and their wives. This folk meaning of drakos as a giant or ogre is well attested in Greek oral tradition.
source: Greek folk oral tradition; Akritas cycle (Hesperia/ASCSA scholarship)
research_notes: Was copy-pasted Drakaina text; rewritten with attested folk drakos (giant/ogre) content.
